sources.citation: Suter, Edgar. 2018. Comparative Morphology of the Huon Peninsula Languages (Papua New Guinea). Inaugural-Dissertation, Universität zu Köln. viii+331 pp. (KUPS 9757)
sources.note: Nothing for Momare. Momare data come from Pilhofer 1928 and unpublished Momare texts collected by Steve McEvoy (SIL, Preface p. iii); the comparative phonology is explicitly unwritten. Only reconstructive asides: Huon Tip emphatic pronouns (incl. Momare ja-haʔ 'himself', na-haʔ 'myself') kept *ja 'presumably because the latter bore a heavy stress on the first syllable in discourse' (p. ~107); Kâte-Mape present tense 'presumably had a unitary word accent on the first syllable of the verb root' (p. ~180) -- diachronic conjectures, not a description of Momare stress.
sources.venue: Inaugural-Dissertation, Universität zu Köln. viii+331 pp. (KUPS 9757)

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1970. Selepet grammar, part I: from root to phrase (with a survey of the Finisterre-Huon languages). PhD thesis, ANU.
sources.note: The stress description (primary stress on the initial syllable of the stress group, secondary stresses on alternate syllables, ch. on phonology/intonation) is for Selepet only. Momare (language 'D') figures only in the Huon Peninsula survey chapter (history: Schmidt's 'Poom' = Momare; lexicostatistics; Eastern Huon Family list).

sources.citation: McEvoy, Steve. 2005. Migabac phonology essentials (in Phonological Descriptions of PNG Languages, SIL-PNG) -- the sister language's description, held in the catalog under miga1241.
sources.note: Describes Migabac stress (sec. 4, primary/secondary levels, alternating pattern); Momare is named only in the Eastern Huon family list (McElhanon 1978); nothing about Momare stress.

sources.citation: Hooley, B. A. & K. A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District, New Guinea. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, 1065-1094. Pacific Linguistics C-13.
sources.note: Nothing. p. 1070: 'The Momare language which is 65 percent related to Kâte is spoken north of the Masaweng River. Although Kâte is well known it appears that Momare will persist for a number of years.'; language table: Momare (350), alt. names Momale/Megabac. Survey only, no phonology.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. Canberra: ANU. 130 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Momare appears only in the Eastern Huon Family language list (p. ~15) and as a wordlist source language; the transcription note (p. 17, 'Deviations from standard phonetic value') covers segments only; a full-text search for stress/accent finds no hit in the whole volume.

sources.citation: Pilhofer, Georg. 1929 [1928-29]. Wörterverzeichnis aus zwölf Mundarten und Nachbarsprachen des Kâte. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 19: 41-69.
sources.note: Companion 300-item comparative wordlist with a Momăle column (breve diacritics visible in snippets); its Vorbemerkung gives transcription conventions and might note accent. Full view on Google Books (sVT-K_-mbmwC) and HathiTrust (uc1.b3347779), could not be reached by automated download.

sources.citation: Pilhofer, Georg. 1928 [1927-28]. Formenlehre von zehn Mundarten und Nachbarsprachen des Kâte. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 18: 196-231, 298-315 (Lautlehre secs. 1-5, pp. 196-199, incl. the Momale diacritic note on p. 199; Momale verb and case paradigms).
sources.note: The only first-hand description of Momare (Momale); its Lautlehre preamble is the one place a Betonung remark could exist (co-occurrence probes suggest there is none, but only reading pp. 196-199 settles it). Public domain, full view from a US browser: HathiTrust uc1.b3347778 / umn.319510018927392 (ZES v.17-18) and Google Books 3CQsswFJepMC -- both could not be reached by automated download.
